extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematics students (especially beginning thesis writers and expositors)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and standards for composing clear mathematical exposition (papers, books, lectures), emphasizing having a clear idea, specifying an audience, organizing material, choosing notation, and careful revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Say Something
rubrics_metrics.description: Have something to say — the piece must have a clear subject (not no ideas or too many ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halmos: "Much bad writing... is caused by a violation of that first principle." He identifies two diseases: (1) saying nothing (no ideas) — text may be grammatical but meaningless (example: Heisel); (2) trying to say too many things — e.g., calculus books mixing many subjects. If the idea is important enough the work may survive poor organization, but generally having a single, unambiguous idea is by far the most important ingredient of good exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak to someone
rubrics_metrics.description: Write for a specific audience — decide who you want to reach and tailor motivation, informality, level of detail, and repetition accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halmos recommends specifying the audience not only broadly (e.g., professional topologists) but as a particular imagined person. This helps anticipate reader difficulties and determine how much motivation and which details to include. He warns against snide remarks or "in" jokes and emphasizes it's better to aim at a definite target than at no target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize first
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize and arrange material before writing: make an outline that lists main headings, lemmas, theorems, corollaries, remarks, and proofs and shows their logical and psychological order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organization minimizes reader resistance and maximizes insight; it indicates emphasis and interconnections. Halmos distinguishes organization (deciding headings and what goes under them) from arrangement (linear ordering). An ideal outline shows where every piece belongs; the organization is often a tree, not a chain. He recommends using slips of paper to play with order during planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a psychological and logical arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange the ordered material so it is both logically correct and psychologically digestible for the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell the reader early what to expect while allowing pleasant, unforeseen surprises; put lemmas where they are needed; use arrangement to hold attention. Organization is more important, but arrangement has psychological value. Halmos gives examples where omitting a section later broke the flow of a course based on a book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize around central examples and counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Center exposition on the concrete examples and counterexamples that motivate and illustrate the theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halmos: "The heart of mathematics consists of concrete examples and concrete problems." Big general theories are usually afterthoughts; insights come from special cases. Structure your work around crucial examples, and guide the reader to what the proofs do not prove and appropriate counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide what to leave out (avoid excessive detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be selective: omit needless detail and over-generalization that add tedium or obfuscation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halmos criticizes over-detailed works (e.g., Bourbaki-style 'dotting the last i') as worse than useless for most serious readers. Too much detail can be as discouraging as none; prepare an outline and make deliberate choices about inclusion and omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think about the alphabet (design notation carefully)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design and standardize notation at the start; choose symbols to avoid conflicts and cognitive dissonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halmos urges investing time to make tables of alphabets and anticipate spaces, groups, vectors, functions, points, measures, etc. Bad ad hoc notation (decisions made mid-sentence) leads to confusion. Examples: avoid conflicting use of Sigma as an index set together with summation notation; aim for 'alphabetical harmony' and avoid 'dissonance'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write, rewrite, and re-rewrite; attend to mechanical details
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that good exposition requires multiple rewrites and attention to diction, notation, punctuation, and other mechanical matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halmos lists writing and re-writing as essential steps and emphasizes willingness to work hard on mechanical details. Careful editing improves clarity even for those with innate expository ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and avoid reader's difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuously try to imagine what in the words may mislead the reader and what will set him right; provide guidance where the reader needs it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping a specific reader in mind helps identify potential confusions; authors should anticipate misunderstandings and insert clarifications, repeats, or alternative proofs where needed rather than leaving the reader to recapitulate discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer organizational coherence over ad hoc patching
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for tight, coherent organization so parts are present because they are needed, and connections are visible rather than relying on ad hoc fixes later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halmos gives an example where skipping a section forced patching and later caused chaos; a well-organized work hides the wires holding it together and makes interconnections apparent. Avoid delivering content in a helter-skelter order that forces later difficult repairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be realistic about outlines and allow for long preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a tentative chapter outline and expect that creating a good outline may take a long time; collect ideas and refine the plan before full composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halmos recommends jotting ideas on slips of paper and assembling them later; often the ideal outline (listing every lemma, theorem, proof) is impossible, but a tentative chapter outline focused on what to include and what to leave out is valuable and may require weeks or years of incubation.
